description_full: BXP, Inc. is the largest publicly traded developer, owner, and manager of premier workplaces in the United States. It is concentrated in six dynamic gateway markets - Boston, Los Angeles, New York, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, DC. BXP has delivered places that power progress for our clients and communities for more than 55 years. BXP is a fully integrated real estate company, organized as a real estate investment trust (REIT). As of June 30, 2026, including properties owned by joint ventures, BXP's portfolio totals 50.6 million square feet and 162 properties, including six properties under construction/redevelopment. BXP's portfolio consists of 141 office properties, 13 retail properties, seven residential properties (including four residential properties under construction) and one hotel. BXP is well known for its in-house building management expertise and responsiveness to clients' needs. BXP holds a superior track record of developing premium Central Business District (CBD) office buildings, successful mixed-use complexes, suburban office centers and build-to-suit projects for a diverse array of creditworthy clients. BXP actively works to promote its growth and operations in a sustainable and responsible manner. BXP, Inc. was incorporated in 1970 in Delaware and is based in Massachusetts, Boston.

Each employee generates $680K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $54K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (9/10).
financial_summary: BXP, Inc. is a large-cap real estate business with a $11.5B market cap on $3.5B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +2.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 61% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $561M in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.50× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.4) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent

Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
28 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Among the least levered in Real Estate — the fortress balance sheet in its peer set

With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.98, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.43 vs 5y 0.97), so read it loosely.

prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It runs a 61% gross margin and converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 4.50x.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.9% over 3 years, 4.7% over 5 years and 3.4% over 10 years.

Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).

It returns 5.6% a year to shareholders (4.4% in dividends).

Short interest is elevated at 10.6% of the float, 8.8 days to cover.
people: With about 826 employees, each generates about $4.2M of revenue, 1.8x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 5.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $680K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.7M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
